```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
library(genevintage)
```

`genevintage` finds the species and the release of a set of gene identifiers
(IDs). This is done by using only the input IDs and the index in the package.
The index has one row for each known release, with data such as the gene count and
the highest ID number.

## Find the species

We start with a small input. `detect_species()` first calculates the fraction of the input that matches the
ID prefix of each species:

```{r frac}
ids <- c(
  "ENSMUSG00000051951", "ENSMUSG00000089699", "ENSMUSG00000051951",
  "TP53"
)
cand <- detect_species(ids)
head(cand[, c("species", "prefix", "frac")])
```

Three of the four inputs have the `ENSMUSG` prefix. All mouse strains share
this prefix, so all have `frac = 0.75`. These rules select between species with
the same `frac`, in this order:

1. Prefix length. A longer prefix gets a higher rank.
2. `reach`. This rule asks if the species can have the highest ID number in
   the input. The package compares this number with the largest `qmax` of the
   species. `qmax` is the highest ID number in a gene set. `QMAX_TOLERANCE`
   sets the permitted difference.
3. `fit`. This rule compares the number of unique IDs with the gene count
   of each release. The smallest difference on a log scale is the `fit`. This
   rule is useful only for a full gene set.

If a tie remains, the species name sets the order. The IDs alone cannot show
the difference between these species. The result does not contain `reach` and
`fit`.

## Find the release

`detect_release()` compares the input with the index. First, it removes each
release that cannot have the input. It uses two facts:

1. ID numbers usually increase. A release older than the highest ID number in
   the input cannot contain that ID.
2. Gene versions also increase. A release older than the highest version in
   the input cannot contain that version.

Ensembl sometimes removes the genes with the highest numbers. This decreases
`qmax`, so `QMAX_TOLERANCE` lets the `qmax` of a release be slightly less
than the highest number in the input. `qmax_violations()` shows each such case
in the index:

```{r violations}
qmax_violations()
```

If a species has a violation, `detect_release()` does not use the first fact
for that species.

We now use a larger input. `dist` ranks the remaining releases:

```{r dist}
ids2 <- readLines(system.file("extdata", "example_ids.txt.gz",
  package = "genevintage"
))
head(detect_release(ids2), 3)
```

`dist` is the absolute difference in `log1p(gene count)` between the input and
the release. Because of the log, one thousand genes have less effect in human
than in a species with a few hundred genes.

If the ID numbers of a species have an order, `dist` also compares the 90th
percentile of the ID numbers. This separates releases with the same gene count
but different ID numbers.

The ID numbers of most schemes that are not Ensembl have no order. For these
schemes, the package does not use the ID number limit or the percentile:

```{r unordered}
head(detect_release(c("YAL001C", "YAL002W", "YAL003W"), species = "yeast"), 5)
```

## GENCODE and Ensembl

The index has Ensembl rows and GENCODE rows for human and mouse. Much RNA-seq
data uses GENCODE, and its gene count is different from Ensembl at the same
release. `detect_release()` ranks the two families together. The `source`
column shows the family of each row.

## Oldest and newest releases

The index covers a fixed range of releases. If your best match is the oldest or
the newest release in this range, be careful. Your IDs can come from a release
outside the range. `detect_release()` gives a warning in this condition.

```{r edge}
head(detect_release(c("ENSG00000141510", "ENSG00000012048"), species = "human"), 3)
```

## Use the functions

Each function below can take a `mapping`, the gene table of one release. We
use the small human table in the package for this vigentte. If you
do not give `mapping`, the function fetches the table from Ensembl. It uses the
`species` and `release` if provided or otherwise infers it from the ID.

```{r map}
hs <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "example_mapping.tsv",
  package = "genevintage"
))
head(hs[, c("id", "name", "chr", "biotype")], 3)
```

`fetch_mapping()` gets the full table of a release. It reads the Ensembl GTF
one time and keeps a copy in the cache:

```r
full <- fetch_mapping("human", release = 116)
dim(full)
#> [1] 78941     9
```

### Change IDs to names

`geneid2name()` keeps the ID of a gene that has no name. The `mapped` attribute
shows the IDs that got a real name:

```{r names}
ids <- c("ENSG00000141510.16", "ENSG00000012048", "ENSG00000284616")
geneid2name(ids, mapping = hs)
```

For a matrix, the function changes the row names:

```{r names-matrix}
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, dimnames = list(ids, c("s1", "s2")))
geneid2name(m, mapping = hs)
```

`gene_ids()` changes names to IDs. `annotate_genes()` gives the full table row
for each ID or name:

```{r lookup}
gene_ids(c("TP53", "BRCA1"), mapping = hs)
annotate_genes(c("TP53", "ENSG00000198804", "MALAT1"), mapping = hs)
```

### Find classes of genes

Each class function returns the genes of one class:

```{r classes}
cols <- c("name", "chr", "biotype")
mito_genes(mapping = hs)[, cols]
sex_genes(mapping = hs, which = "Y")[, cols]
ribosomal_genes(mapping = hs)[, cols]
hemoglobin_genes(mapping = hs)[, cols]
mhc_genes(mapping = hs)[, cols]
```

Other functions return RNA classes and biotypes:

```{r rna}
trna_genes(mapping = hs)[, cols]
rrna_genes(mapping = hs)[, cols]
lncrna_genes(mapping = hs)[, cols]
genes_by_biotype("pseudogene", mapping = hs)[, cols]
table(noncoding_genes(mapping = hs)$biotype)
gene_biotypes(mapping = hs)
```

If you give IDs or names, the function keeps only those in the class. The
`input` column holds your values, so you can use it to select matrix rows:

```{r input}
coding_genes(c("TP53", "MALAT1", "XIST"), mapping = hs)[, c("input", cols)]
counts <- matrix(1:72, ncol = 2, dimnames = list(hs$id, c("s1", "s2")))
mt <- mito_genes(rownames(counts), mapping = hs)
colSums(counts[mt$input, ]) / colSums(counts) # mitochondrial fraction
```

The sex chromosomes come from the annotation. Chicken has Z and W:

```r
sex_genes(species = "chicken", which = "W", release = 116)[1:3, cols]
#> gallus_gallus, ensembl release 116
#>      name chr        biotype
#> 1    <NA>   W protein_coding
#> 2    <NA>   W protein_coding
#> 3 UBAP2L2   W protein_coding
```

### Repair excel corruputed gene names

Excel changes `SEPT9` to `9-Sep` and `DEC1` to `1-Dec`. `correct_genenames()`
can fix these corruptions. It changes a name only if one gene in the table fits:

```{r excel}
x <- c("9-Sep", "1-Dec", "1-Mar", "TP53")
fixed <- correct_genenames(x, mapping = hs)
as.vector(fixed)
attr(fixed, "ambiguous")
```

`1-Mar` can be `MARCHF1` or `MTARC1`, so it stays unchanged. An older release
gives the older names:

```r
as.vector(correct_genenames(c("9-Sep", "1-Dec"),
  species = "human", release = 95, quiet = TRUE
))
#> [1] "SEPT9" "DEC1"
```

### Change transcripts to genes

`transcript2gene()` gives the gene of each transcript. `aggregate_transcripts()`
adds the counts of the transcripts of each gene:

```{r tx}
tx <- data.frame(
  transcript_id = c("ENST00000269305", "ENST00000357654"),
  id = c("ENSG00000141510", "ENSG00000012048"), name = c("TP53", "BRCA1")
)
tx_ids <- c("ENST00000269305.9", "ENST00000357654.9")
transcript2gene(tx_ids, mapping = tx)
tc <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2, dimnames = list(tx_ids, c("s1", "s2")))
aggregate_transcripts(tc, mapping = tx)
```

Without `mapping`, the function finds the species and release from the IDs:

```r
transcript2gene(c("ENSMUST00000178537.2", "ENSMUST00000178862.2"))
#> mus_musculus, ensembl release 116 (assembly 39): 2 of 2 transcripts mapped
#>                  input      transcript_id            gene_id gene_name
#> 1 ENSMUST00000178537.2 ENSMUST00000178537 ENSMUSG00000095668     Trbd1
#> 2 ENSMUST00000178862.2 ENSMUST00000178862 ENSMUSG00000094569     Trbd2
```

### Use Ensembl data

These functions read Ensembl files, so they need a network connection.
`orthologs()` reads Ensembl Compara. `ortholog_species()` lists the species
that Compara covers:

```r
orthologs(c("ENSG00000141510", "ENSG00000012048"), to = "mouse", release = 116)
#>                id  name        ortholog_id ortholog_name    homology_type
#> 1 ENSG00000012048 BRCA1 ENSMUSG00000017146         Brca1 ortholog_one2one
#> 2 ENSG00000141510  TP53 ENSMUSG00000059552         Trp53 ortholog_one2one
#>   identity ortholog_identity high_confidence
#> 1  56.0923           57.6711            TRUE
#> 2  77.3537           77.9487            TRUE
```

`compare_releases()` gives the genes that changed between two releases:

```r
d <- compare_releases("human", from = 110, to = 116)
#> homo_sapiens 110 -> 116: 17456 added, 1269 removed, 1403 renamed, 1370 retyped
```

`entrez_ids()` gives the Entrez ID of each gene. `gene_lengths()` gives the
exon-union length, which TPM and FPKM need:

```r
entrez_ids(c("TP53", "BRCA1"), species = "human", release = 116)
#> homo_sapiens, ensembl release 116
#>   input              id  name entrez
#> 1  TP53 ENSG00000141510  TP53   7157
#> 2 BRCA1 ENSG00000012048 BRCA1    672
gene_lengths("human", release = 116, ids = c("ENSG00000141510", "ENSG00000012048"))
#> ENSG00000141510 ENSG00000012048 
#>            8043           14232
```

The `fetch_*()` and `stream_*()` functions read the Ensembl files that these
functions use. `gene_cache()` lists the cached files, and
`gene_cache(clear = TRUE)` removes them.

### Species and identifier schemes

`resolve_species()` changes a common name to an Ensembl name.
`species_table()` lists the names:

```{r species}
resolve_species("Norway rat")
species_table("zebrafish")
```

`parse_ens()` splits Ensembl IDs into their parts. `guess_scheme()` finds the
scheme of a set of IDs:

```{r parse}
parse_ens(c("ENSG00000141510.16", "ENSMUST00000178537.2"))
guess_scheme(c("FBgn0000008", "FBgn0000014", "FBgn0000015"))$scheme
```

Gene names do not have a prefix. `detect_species_names()` calculates 
scores for each species based on overlapping index. You can generate 
the index yourself:

```{r symbols}
ix <- build_symbol_index(transform(hs, species = "homo_sapiens", release = "116"))
symbols <- c("TP53", "BRCA1", "GAPDH", "ACTB", "XIST", "HBB", "MALAT1", "PTPRC")
detect_species_names(symbols, ix, min_overlap = 5)
```
